title: Introduction to the Welding Shop (Hot Shop) Practice

content.aim: To study the principles of welding, the types of welding joint, welding positions, arc welding equipment and processes, and the safety recommendations for arc welding.
objectives: To know how to prepare welding edges before welding.
To know the different welding joints and welding positions.
To know the various arc welding processes and equipment.
To know the safety recommendations for arc welding.
To produce a butt joint using arc welding.
apparatus: Arc welding machine (air-cooled transformer type) with electrode holder and earth clamp.
Mild steel electrodes, 3.1 mm x 350 mm.
Welding table (metallic), tongs, chipping hammer and wire brush.
Face shield or hand shield, apron, asbestos or leather gloves, protective clothing.
Mild steel plates, rough and smooth files.

theory.text:
Welding is a process for joining two similar or dissimilar metals or alloys by fusion. It joins different metals with or without the application of pressure and with or without the use of filler metal. The fusion of the metal takes place through heat, which may be generated by the combustion of gases, an electric arc, electric resistance or chemical reaction. Welding provides a permanent joint, but it normally affects the metallurgy of the components, and so it is usually accompanied by post-weld heat treatment for most critical components. Welding is widely used as a fabrication and repair process in industry, for example in ships, pressure vessels, automobile bodies, offshore platforms, bridges and welded pipes. The term weldability is the property of a metal which indicates the ease with which it can be welded with other similar or dissimilar metals. The terms used for describing a weld are shown in the figure: the base metal, fusion zone, weld face, root face, root opening, toe and root.

Edge preparation

For welding, the surfaces to be joined are prepared first. Different edge preparations are used for welding butt joints, depending on plate thickness: straight (square), single-V, double-V, single-U, double-U, single-J, double-J, single-bevel and double-bevel. The purpose is to allow the weld metal to reach the root of the joint and give full penetration.

Welding joints

Welding joints are generally of two kinds, the lap joint and the butt joint. A single-lap joint is made by overlapping the edges of the plates; it has very little resistance to bending and is not recommended for most work. A double-lap joint is stronger but requires twice as much welding. The tee fillet weld is widely used but should not be used if an alternative design is possible. The butt weld includes the single-vee butt weld, used for plates up to about 15.8 mm thick with the plates spaced about 3.2 mm apart, and the double-vee butt weld for plates over 13 mm thick where welding can be done on both sides.

Welding positions

There are four welding positions. In the flat or downhand position, the welding is done from the upper side of the joint and the face of the weld is approximately horizontal. In the horizontal position, the plane of the work is vertical and the deposited weld bead is horizontal. This is commonly used in welding vessels and reservoirs. In the vertical position, the plane of the work is vertical and the weld is deposited upon a vertical surface; it is difficult to produce satisfactory welds because gravity acts on the molten metal. The overhead position is even more difficult because the pull of gravity against the molten metal is much greater.

Arc welding process

In arc welding an electric arc is established between an electrode and the work piece to melt the base metals. The arc temperature is very high, which melts the electrode tip and the parent metal, forming a weld pool that solidifies into the weld bead. Some processes use a shielding gas, and others use flux coatings to protect the molten pool from the atmosphere, and to stabilise the arc. The equipment includes a switch box, secondary terminals, the welding machine, a current reading scale and a current-regulating hand wheel. The operator's accessories are the leather apron, asbestos gloves, protective glasses or face shield, electrode holder, chipping hammer, wire brush, earth clamp and a welding table. The power source may be alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC). DC welding is usually obtained from generators driven by electric motors or by internal combustion engines. Where mains supply is available, transformers are used for AC welding to step down the supply voltage (200 to 400 V) to the open-circuit welding voltage (50 to 90 V). The choice of power source depends on the type of electrode and metal, the available supply, the output needed, the duty cycle, efficiency, cost, floor space and versatility. Welding cables carry the current from the power source through the electrode holder, the arc, the work piece and back to the machine; they are insulated copper or aluminium cables. The electrode holder holds the electrode and conducts current to it, with sizes from 150 to 500 A. Welding electrodes are consumable (bare or coated) or non-consumable (carbon or tungsten). In a consumable electrode the tip melts and supplies filler metal. The flux coating on a coated electrode melts to give a gas shield, removes impurities as slag and stabilises the arc. Non-consumable electrodes, made of carbon or tungsten, do not melt appreciably.

Safety recommendations

The welding machine frame must be earthed. The arc produces infrared and ultraviolet light, so the operator must use a helmet or hand shield fitted with a special filter glass. Excess ultraviolet light can cause an effect like sunburn on the skin. The body is protected from sparks and molten metal by gloves, a leather apron and, for overhead work, a leather skull cap and jackets. Equipment should be inspected periodically and kept in safe working condition.

procedure: We were introduced to the welding shop and given a safety briefing.
The welding terms, edge preparations, joints and positions were explained with examples.
The arc welding machine and its accessories were identified and their functions explained.
The correct use of the protective clothing, face shield and gloves was demonstrated.
A demonstration of striking an arc, running a bead, chipping the slag and cleaning was given by the instructor.
precautions: Always wear a face shield with a filter glass, gloves and an apron.
Never look at the arc with the naked eye, and keep other people shielded from it.
Make sure that the machine is earthed and the cables are not damaged.
Do not weld on wet floors and keep flammable materials away from the area.
Use tongs to handle hot work, and wear safety glasses when chipping the slag.
content.discussion: The welding shop showed us how many different factors influence a sound weld: the edge preparation, the position, the electrode, the current and the skill of the welder. We understood why plates are bevelled for thick sections, since the weld metal has to reach the root of the joint for full penetration. The flat position is the easiest because gravity helps to keep the weld pool in place, whereas overhead welding requires much more skill. The safety recommendations are particularly important because the dangers of arc welding are not always obvious. Ultraviolet light from the arc can burn the skin and eyes in a short time, and metal spatter and hot slag can cause burns, so full protective clothing is required.
content.conclusion: The principles of welding, the types of joint, edge preparation, welding positions, equipment, electrodes and safety rules for arc welding were studied. This provides the necessary background for the practical butt and lap joints.

questions.question: What is welding?
questions.answer: A process for joining two similar or dissimilar metals by fusion, with or without pressure and with or without filler metal.

questions.question: Why is the coating on an electrode important?
questions.answer: It protects the molten pool from the atmosphere, stabilises the arc and forms slag that protects the cooling weld.

learnings: The meaning of welding, weldability and the terms used for a weld.
The difference between lap and butt joints and the types of edge preparation.
The equipment of an arc welding set and how the arc circuit works.
The safety precautions that protect a welder from light, heat and electricity.
